Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Ethan was thirty-two years old, a tutor who worked mostly from home, but it hadn't always been that way. A year ago, he had taken a position at a community learning centre, where he helped adults prepare for their high school equivalency exams. One of his students, a man in his late forties, had been struggling with the material and became increasingly frustrated. Ethan remembered the first time the man raised his voice—a sharp, scornful tone during a session—and Ethan had tried to calm him, but the anger only seemed to deepen. A week later, Ethan found a note on his car: *You think you're better than me?* He dismissed it as stress. Then the calls started—late at night, the same voice, angry and accusing. Ethan changed his number, but the calls found him anyway. He began to notice a motorcycle idling outside his apartment, sometimes revving loudly at odd hours. He knew it was him. He saw the same figure parked across the street, watching. The feeling of being followed became a daily certainty, a shadow that never quite disappeared. He reported it to the police, but without a clear threat they could not act. The stalking went on for three months, then stopped almost as abruptly as it had begun—the man moved away, Ethan heard. But the damage had already settled into his bones.

In the months that followed, Ethan found himself unable to trust the quiet. He stopped going anywhere he had not been before. He would drive extra miles to avoid an unfamiliar street, certain that he could not assess the danger in a place he did not already know. His wife, Rachel, asked why he no longer wanted to try new restaurants, why he insisted on the same route to the grocery store. Ethan told her it was just preference, but inside he was afraid that if something happened, he would not know where to run. Relaxation felt impossible—sitting still, letting his guard down, felt like inviting disaster. He had begun to believe he deserved to suffer, that maybe he had provoked the man somehow, that if he had been more careful or less dismissive the whole thing could have been avoided. That thought sat heavy in his chest, and he did not push it away.

His sleep fractured. He lay awake for hours, listening for a motorcycle that never came, or he startled awake from shallow dreams with his heart pounding. Rachel would reach for him in the dark, and he would freeze, not wanting her to touch him. Intimacy had become a risk he could not take. He was certain that if he let himself be close to her, if he relaxed into her warmth, something terrible would happen. He did not say this to her; he just turned away and pretended to be tired.

At work, he stopped taking new clients. He tutored only returning students, people he already knew. The moment a parent expressed frustration over a missed appointment, even calmly, Ethan's throat tightened and his mind went blank. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed—that a pleasant face could hide a dangerous anger, that everyone had a breaking point he might trigger. He no longer trusted his own judgment. He doubted every decision, every word he said, replaying conversations for signs that he had offended someone.

A few weeks before he finally sought help, a neighbor across the hall raised his voice on the phone—nothing directed at Ethan, just a heated argument with a relative. Ethan froze in his doorway, heart hammering, convinced for a full minute that the man was coming for him. He stood there, useless, ready to run. That was the moment he knew he could not keep living this way. He made an appointment with a therapist, terrified that she too might turn out to be someone else, but more terrified of the life he was building—one of solitude, suspicion, and a silence that felt like waiting for the next blow.
